nameStory: This handsome duck bears the name of Sir John Barrow, a British geographer and Arctic explorer from the early 1800s. The 'goldeneye' part comes from the bird's striking bright yellow eyes that seem to glow like golden coins against its dark head.
description: Barrow's Goldeneye is a medium-sized diving duck with a distinctive bulbous, rounded head that gives it a somewhat top-heavy appearance. Males sport a glossy purple-black head with a distinctive white crescent-shaped patch near the bill, while females have warm brown heads. Both sexes flash bright golden-yellow eyes and show bold white patches on their wings when flying. They're stocky, compact ducks built for diving underwater to hunt for food.

idTips.label: Head shape
idTips.description: Distinctly bulbous, rounded head that looks almost oversized for the body, giving the duck a unique profile both on water and in flight

idTips.label: Male head pattern
idTips.description: Glossy purple-black head with a white crescent or comma-shaped patch in front of the bright yellow eye

idTips.label: Golden eyes
idTips.description: Brilliant yellow-gold eyes that catch the light and stand out dramatically against the dark head feathers

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Bold white patches on the wings create a striking contrast when the bird takes flight or stretches

idTips.label: Diving behavior
idTips.description: Disappears completely underwater with a forward-diving motion, staying submerged for 15-30 seconds while hunting

habitat: In New England, Barrow's Goldeneyes are rare winter visitors to coastal waters, rocky shorelines, and occasionally large inland lakes and reservoirs. They prefer areas with clear, deep water where they can dive for mollusks, crustaceans, and aquatic insects. Look for them around jetties, harbors, and protected bays along the Maine coast.

seasonality.spring: Occasional sightings during migration in March and April as birds head north to their breeding grounds. Males may still show their full breeding plumage during early spring visits.
seasonality.summer: Extremely rare in New England during summer months, as they breed far to the north and west in Canada and Alaska.
seasonality.fall: First winter arrivals may appear in late November, though sightings remain uncommon. Birds are transitioning to winter plumage.
seasonality.winter: Peak season for New England sightings from December through February, when they visit coastal waters. Males display full breeding colors during this time.

funFact: Despite being called a 'goldeneye,' young Barrow's Goldeneyes actually have gray eyes that don't turn their signature brilliant yellow-gold color until they're almost a year old!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the much more common Common Goldeneye. Look for Barrow's more triangular white face patch (vs. Common's round white spot) and steeper forehead profile. Remember: Barrow's has a 'boomerang' patch, Common has a 'coin' patch.
contextualKnowledge: Though named after an English explorer, Barrow's Goldeneyes are primarily western North American birds. Seeing one in New England is quite special, as they're far from their normal range along the Pacific coast and interior west.
compareHints: Compared to Common Goldeneye, Barrow's has a more triangular white face patch, steeper forehead, and slightly larger overall size. Unlike the smaller, more compact Bufflehead in the same genus, Barrow's Goldeneye lacks the puffy, cotton-ball head shape and has a much more prominent white wing patch. Both male goldeneye species show much more white on the body than the predominantly dark Bufflehead.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Buffleheads are much smaller than their goldeneye cousins and have that distinctive puffy, rounded head shape.
Common Goldeneyes are much larger than their Bufflehead cousins and have different head patterns - males lack the Bufflehead's white head patch that wraps around the back of the head.
